body.heading: The urge to step in
paragraphs: Watching a child slowly pour their own drink, button their own coat, or carry their own plate takes a particular kind of patience. Every adult instinct says it would be quicker and drier to do it yourself. Often it would be. That is not the same as it being better.
Children learn a task by doing it badly within sight of someone calm. Spills, wonky buttons, and slow zips are the curriculum, not interruptions to it.

body.heading: Make the environment forgiving
paragraphs: You can stack the odds without taking over: small jugs instead of full ones, clothes with fastenings they can manage, a cloth kept nearby for spills so a spill is a wipe, not an event. Forgiveness built into the setup means you have to supply less of it yourself.
Start with tasks where the stakes are low and time is plentiful — weekend mornings, not school-run mornings. Independence practised under no pressure becomes independence available under pressure.

body.heading: Stand back, stay close
paragraphs: The helpful position is nearby and available, not hovering and correcting. Answer questions, admire the result, and let them feel the full weight of 'I did it myself' — which is heavier, and better, than any praise.

description: Letting children do things themselves is slower and messier in the moment, and it is exactly how they become capable.
